## Introduction

High-end AI accelerators like the AMD Instinct MI300X pack an incredible amount of compute power and memory. However, dedicating an entire physical GPU to a single, lightweight inference workload often means leaving expensive resources sitting idle. In a multi-tenant cluster, this underutilization is costly and wasteful.

GPU partitioning solves this problem by allowing you to slice a single physical GPU into multiple,  isolated devices. This learning path shows you how to transition your systems from a default unpartitioned state SPX (no partitions) to a maximum multi-tenancy configuration that uses Core Partition X (CPX) and Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) Per Socket (NPS) 4 (NPS4). By the end of this learning path, you will be able to multiply your workload density—getting more out of your infrastructure investments.

## Prerequisites:

Before beginning the GPU partitioning procedure, ensure your environment meets the following requirements:

* **Hardware**: A system with AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs.  
* **Firmware/VBIOS**: For MI300X systems, the minimal VBIOS version supported for partitioning is 022.040.003.042 (see [official docs](https://instinct.docs.amd.com/projects/amdgpu-docs/en/latest/gpu-partitioning/mi300x/requirements.html#c-firmware-requirements)). It is highly recommended to update to the latest firmware and BIOS versions from your vendor, especially if some available partitions are not displaying.  
* **Cluster environment**: A  single-node OpenShift cluster or a multi-node Red Hat OpenShift environment.  
* **Required components**: The AMD GPU Operator (and [dependencies](https://instinct.docs.amd.com/projects/gpu-operator/en/latest/installation/openshift-olm.html)) must be installed, as the device config manager (DCM) is a component of this operator.  
* **Storage (optional)**: If you plan to run the vLLM validation workload and want to store the model cache via a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC), you will need a storage backend configured, such as LVMS.  
* **Credentials (optional)**: A Hugging Face token stored as a Kubernetes Secret is required only if you intend to deploy and access gated models during the validation step.

## In this learning path, you will:

* Understand the concepts of GPU partitioning and the specific compute (CPX) and memory (NPS) pairings required for AMD Instinct accelerators.  
* Configure the AMD device config manager (DCM) by creating Kubernetes-native partition profiles and manifests.  
* Implement node taints and tolerations to safely isolate control plane workloads while reconfiguring hardware resources.  
* Execute hardware-level partitioning to transform a single physical GPU into multiple isolated logical devices.  
* Deploy a vLLM inference server to a partitioned GPU slice to validate your configuration.

### GPU partitioning with DCM 

The device config manager (DCM) is a component of the GPU operator that is used to handle the configuration and partitioning of AMD Instinct GPUs.

The current goal of the DCM is to handle the configuration and implementation of GPU partitioning on your Kubernetes cluster, allowing for partitioning modes to be set on each GPU node based on partition profiles that you specify via a Kubernetes ConfigMap (see [official docs](https://instinct.docs.amd.com/projects/gpu-operator/en/latest/dcm/device-config-manager.html)).

By default, MI300X systems initially start in SPX mode (no partitions), as shown below in Figure 1\.  
![][image1]  
Figure 1: AMD Instinct MI300X System configured in SPX and NPS1 mode (no partitions).

Alt text: A Grafana "AMD Instinct Single Node Dashboard" for a Dell PowerEdge XE9680 with 8 AMD MI300X GPUs, showing all GPUs at 0% utilization, low memory usage (i.e., 0.144% and 283 MB each), all healthy (green), with power draw around 150–163 W per GPU and temperatures in the 41–51°C range at idle.

In this learning path, we show you how to configure partitioning for optimal multi-tenant use cases (i.e., CPX \+ NPS4 pairing) in single-node OpenShift.

# Lesson 1: Add tolerations to protect critical control plane workloads 

| Title *Describes job to be done* | Add tolerations to protect critical control plane workloads  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Meta description** *160-character max summary of what they will learn, what will show in search engines* | Patch critical Red Hat OpenShift control plane workloads with tolerations to survive taints applied during GPU partitioning. |
| **Topics** | Artificial intelligence |
| **Products used in this lesson** | Red Hat OpenShift |
| **Lesson completion time** |  |

## Introduction

AMD GPUs cannot be partitioned while workloads are running; so we need to bring down all DaemonSets using the GPU resource before partitioning. To do so, add tolerations to all deployments and DaemonSets in critical control plane namespaces. 

Tolerations allow control plane pods to survive an `amd-dcm=up:NoExecute` taint applied to the node when enabling GPU partitioning. This prevents accidental eviction of essential control plane workloads from the GPU node.

We will use the toleration that is pre-configured by default in the device config manager (DCM) pod.

## Prerequisites

* Full cluster administrator privileges on your Red Hat OpenShift environment.  
* The `jq` command-line utility installed locally for processing JSON patches.

## In this lesson, you will:

* Map the critical infrastructure namespaces required for node connectivity and machine management in Red Hat OpenShift.  
* Execute automated shell scripts to apply live JSON schema patches across cluster control plane deployments.

## Add tolerations

1. To prepare your environment, define the DCM toleration:

```
TOLERATION='[{"key": "amd-dcm", "operator": "Equal", "value": "up", "effect": "NoExecute"}]'
```

2. Execute the following bash block to stage the control plane environment namespaces (e.g., Red Hat OpenShift 4.20 release). 

   **Note:** The list of Red Hat OpenShift namespaces for cluster operators and critical components could change from release to release. Always verify against your cluster.

```
CONTROL_PLANE_NAMESPACES=(
  # Networking (CRITICAL - node connectivity)
  "openshift-ovn-kubernetes"
  "openshift-multus"
  "openshift-dns"
  "openshift-dns-operator"
  "openshift-network-operator"
  "openshift-network-diagnostics"
  "openshift-network-node-identity"
  "openshift-network-console"

  # Machine/Node management
  "openshift-machine-config-operator"
  "openshift-machine-api"
  "openshift-cluster-node-tuning-operator"
  "openshift-cluster-machine-approver"

  # API servers and authentication (CRITICAL)
  "openshift-kube-apiserver"
  "openshift-kube-apiserver-operator"
  "openshift-apiserver"
  "openshift-apiserver-operator"
  "openshift-oauth-apiserver"
  "openshift-authentication"
  "openshift-authentication-operator"

  # Controllers (CRITICAL)
  "openshift-kube-controller-manager"
  "openshift-kube-controller-manager-operator"
  "openshift-kube-scheduler"
  "openshift-kube-scheduler-operator"
  "openshift-controller-manager"
  "openshift-controller-manager-operator"
  "openshift-route-controller-manager"

  # Cluster operators (CRITICAL)
  "openshift-cluster-version"
  "openshift-config-operator"
  "openshift-etcd"
  "openshift-etcd-operator"

  # Cloud and cluster services
  "openshift-cloud-controller-manager-operator"
  "openshift-cloud-credential-operator"
  "openshift-cluster-samples-operator"
  "openshift-service-ca"
  "openshift-service-ca-operator"
  "openshift-insights"
)
```

3. Add tolerations to selected components:

```
# sample pseudocode (no actual code)

for ns in $CONTROL_PLANE_NAMESPACES; do

  # Patch deployments
  oc get deployments -n "$ns" -o json 2>/dev/null | \
    jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name' | \
    xargs -I {} oc patch deployment {} -n "$ns" --type='json' \
    -p='[{"op": "add", "path": "/spec/template/spec/tolerations", "value": '"$TOLERATION"'}]'

  # Patch daemonsets
  oc get daemonsets -n "$ns" -o json 2>/dev/null | \
    jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name' | \
    xargs -I {} oc patch daemonset {} -n "$ns" --type='json' \
    -p='[{"op": "add", "path": "/spec/template/spec/tolerations", "value": '"$TOLERATION"'}]'

  # Patch statefulsets
  oc get statefulsets -n "$ns" -o json 2>/dev/null | \
    jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name' | \
    xargs -I {} oc patch statefulset {} -n "$ns" --type='json' \
    -p='[{"op": "add", "path": "/spec/template/spec/tolerations", "value": '"$TOLERATION"'}]

done
```

You have successfully insulated your critical Red Hat OpenShift routing, storage, API, and orchestration layers. The pods running in these namespaces can now survive the automated eviction procedures that occur when the physical host undergoes its hardware re-partitioning.

Now that you have added tolerations, let’s deploy the device config manager (DCM).

# Lesson 2: Configure and deploy the device config manager 

| Title *Describes job to be done* | Configure and deploy the device config manager  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Meta description** *160-character max summary of what they will learn, what will show in search engines* | Create custom GPU partition profiles via a ConfigMap and enable the device config manager to orchestrate hardware partitioning in Red Hat OpenShift. |
| **Topics** | Artificial intelligence |
| **Products used in this lesson** | Red Hat OpenShift |
| **Lesson completion time** |  |

## Introduction

Now that your control-plane workloads are protected with tolerations, you can prepare the infrastructure components that control the accelerator devices. The AMD GPU Operator manages these hardware day2 operations using a component called the device config manager (DCM).

By default, the DCM is not active. To enable it, define a ConfigMap that maps partition profiles to your hardware—for example, a single monolithic GPU (SPX) or multiple smaller slices (CPX)—so the operator knows which compute and memory layout to apply on each node. 

GPU Partition Info (reference from node):

- Available compute partitions: SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX  
- Available memory partitions: NPS1, NPS2, NPS4

## Prerequisites

* Tolerations (lesson 1).   
* The AMD GPU Operator installed in the `openshift-amd-gpu` namespace.

## In this lesson, you will:

* Create a ConfigMap with GPU partition profiles  
* Patch the DeviceConfig custom resource to enable and configure the device config manager,  which orchestrates GPU partitioning.

## Deploy DCM 

1. Validate the available compute and memory partitions that your target GPU node supports with the command below. 

```
cat /sys/module/amdgpu/drivers/pci\:amdgpu/*/{available_compute_partition,available_memory_partition}

```

   On a standard AMD Instinct MI300X system with an 8-GPU layout, your output will look like this:

   `SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX`

   `SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX`

   `SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX`

   `SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX`

   `SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX`

   `SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX`

   `SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX`

   `SPX, DPX, QPX, CPX`

   `NPS1, NPS2, NPS4`

   `NPS1, NPS2, NPS4`

   `NPS1, NPS2, NPS4`

   `NPS1, NPS2, NPS4`

   `NPS1, NPS2, NPS4`

   `NPS1, NPS2, NPS4`

   `NPS1, NPS2, NPS4`

   `NPS1, NPS2, NPS4`

   **Note**: If some of the available partitions are not shown in your MI300X series systems (e.g., NPS2), it is recommended to update to the latest Firmware and BIOS versions from your vendor. For the MI300X system, the minimal VBIOS version supported for partitioning is 022.040.003.042.

2. Create DCM profiles via ConfigMap. This configuration outlines three distinct infrastructure choices: a standard unpartitioned blueprint (`spx-profile-nps1`), a dual setup (`dpx-profile-nps2`), and the high-density quad-compute option (`cpx-profile-nps4`). Run the command below to build and apply the configuration to your cluster.

```
cat <<EOF | tee gpu-partition-profiles.yaml | oc apply -f -
---apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: config-manager-config
  namespace: openshift-amd-gpu
data:
  config.json: |
    {
      "gpu-config-profiles": {
        "spx-profile-nps1": {
          "skippedGPUs": {
            "ids": []
          },
          "profiles": [
            {
              "computePartition": "SPX",
              "memoryPartition": "NPS1",
              "numGPUsAssigned": 8
            }
          ]
        },
        "dpx-profile-nps2": {
          "skippedGPUs": {
            "ids": []
          },
          "profiles": [
            {
              "computePartition": "DPX",
              "memoryPartition": "NPS2",
              "numGPUsAssigned": 8
            }
          ]
        },
        "cpx-profile-nps4": {
          "skippedGPUs": {
            "ids": []
          },
          "profiles": [
            {
              "computePartition": "CPX",
              "memoryPartition": "NPS4",
              "numGPUsAssigned": 8
            }
          ]
        }
      },
      "gpuClientSystemdServices": {
        "names": ["amd-metrics-exporter", "gpuagent"]
      }
    }
EOF

```

3. Modify the AMD GPU Operator configuration to read your newly created file and enable DCM.

```
oc patch deviceconfig amdgpu-driver-install -n openshift-amd-gpu --type='merge' -p '{
  "spec": {
    "configManager": {
      "enable": true,
      "image": "docker.io/rocm/device-config-manager:v1.4.1",
      "imagePullPolicy": "IfNotPresent",
      "config": {
        "name": "config-manager-config"
      }
    }
  }
}'
```

4. ### To determine which DCM versions are publicly available, you can use [Skopeo](https://github.com/containers/skopeo) to list the tags released by AMD.

```
skopeo list-tags docker://docker.io/rocm/device-config-manager
{
    "Repository": "docker.io/rocm/device-config-manager",
    "Tags": [
        "v1.3.0",
        "v1.3.0-beta.0",
        "v1.3.1",
        "v1.3.1-beta.0",
        "v1.4.0",
        "v1.4.0-beta.0",
        "v1.4.1"
    ]
}
```

5. ### Wait for the DCM pod to be ready:

```
oc wait --for=condition=ready pod \
  -l app.kubernetes.io/name=device-config-manager \
  -n openshift-amd-gpu \
  --timeout=300s
```

You have verified your host system's hardware options, deployed a configuration layout to your cluster, and deployed the DCM. 

In the next lesson, you will trigger the active hardware transition by applying structural taints and labeling your GPU node to execute the partitioning process.

# Lesson 3: Taint and label GPU node 

| Title *Describes job to be done* | Taint and label GPU node to trigger AMD hardware partitioning |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Meta description** *160-character max summary of what they will learn, what will show in search engines* |  |
| **Topics** | Artificial intelligence |
| **Products used in this lesson** | Red Hat OpenShift |
| **Lesson completion time** |  |

## Introduction

With your control plane protected and the device config manager (DCM) deployed, you are ready to begin partitioning. Slicing an AMD Instinct GPU requires resetting the underlying device. Because of this, you must clear the target node of all active workloads so that no applications are left trying to use the hardware when the configuration change occurs.

Tainting the GPU node with `amd-dcm=up:NoExecute` will immediately evict all non-essential workloads and prevent the scheduling of new workloads on the node. This ensures no workloads are using the GPUs before partitioning. Only pods and DaemonSets with the matching toleration will remain running.

We will then label the node with the desired partition profile, which signals DCM to apply the GPU partitioning configuration. 

## Prerequisites

* Apply tolerations (lesson 1).    
* Configure and deploy the device config manager (lesson 2). 

## In this lesson, you will:

* Apply a node taint to safely evict active user workloads from your GPU host.  
* Apply a custom configuration label to trigger the automated hardware-level partitioning routine.

## Taint and label the GPU node 

1. ### Taint GPU node to evict non-essential workloads. Run the following command:

```
oc taint nodes "$NODE_NAME" amd-dcm=up:NoExecute
```

2. After tainting the node, inspect the status of all pods in the cluster. In your environment, the Prometheus exporter pod enters an `Error` state (not `Pending`) and continues holding GPU resources, which blocks the DCM partitioning process. To unblock it, scale down the Prometheus instance and force-delete the stuck pod: 

```
oc patch prometheus amd-gpu-prometheus -n devmetrics --type='merge' -p '{"spec":{"replicas":0}}'

oc delete pod -n devmetrics prometheus-amd-gpu-prometheus-0 --force --grace-period=0
```

3. With the drivers clear, tell the DCM to apply the GPU partitioning configuration by labeling your node with your desired target profile name and partitioning profile.

   **Note**: The \--overwrite flag accounts for any existing `gpu-config-profile` label.

```
oc label node $NODE_NAME dcm.amd.com/gpu-config-profile=cpx-profile-nps4 --overwrite
```

4. Wait for DCM to process the profile:

```
oc logs -n openshift-amd-gpu -l app.kubernetes.io/name=device-config-manager -f
```

   A successful output will look like this:

   `NEW TRIGGER ALERT FROM NODE LABELS`

   `2026/05/27 09:10:48 Label changed: dcm.amd.com/gpu-config-profile`

   `Old value:` 

   `New value: cpx-profile-nps4`

   `2026/05/27 09:10:48 #####################################`

   `2026/05/27 09:10:48 Partition profile info:`

   `2026/05/27 09:10:48 Selected profile name: cpx-profile-nps4`

   `2026/05/27 09:10:48 #####################################`

   

   `. . . TRUNCATED . . .`

   

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 Successfully Partitioned GPUs of profile 1`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 Partition completed successfully`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 Label "dcm.amd.com/gpu-config-profile-state" added successfully to node "smc6216gpu.partner-accelerators.redhat.lab"`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 AMD SMI shutdown successfully`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 #####################################`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 PartitionGPU executed successfully`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 ServicesList [amd-metrics-exporter gpuagent]`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 Restarting service skipped for: amd-metrics-exporter.service (was not-loaded at 2026-05-27 09:10:58.654388053 +0000 UTC m=+45.487989488)`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 Restarting service skipped for: gpuagent.service (was not-loaded at 2026-05-27 09:11:08.663196594 +0000 UTC m=+55.496798039)`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 Cleaning up PreStateDB...`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 PreStateDB has been successfully emptied.`

   `2026/05/27 09:12:10 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^`

   

   

5. Once DCM has completed the partitioning procedure, it labels the node with the result of that operation:

```
oc get nodes -o json | jq '.items[].metadata.labels | with_entries(select(.key | startswith("dcm.amd.com")))'


```

   	  
   Your output will look like this:

     `"dcm.amd.com/gpu-config-profile": "cpx-profile-nps4",`

     `"dcm.amd.com/gpu-config-profile-state": "success"`

Success\! You’ve tainted and labeled the GPU node, triggering the DCM to partition your hardware accelerator into a custom layout. The orchestration layer has completed its backend tasks.

Now it’s time to verify your new GPU partitioning. 

# Lesson 4: Verify GPU partitioning 

| Title *Describes job to be done* | Verify GPU partitioning  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Meta description** *160-character max summary of what they will learn, what will show in search engines* | Use the device config manager pod to verify that your single GPU node has successfully partitioned. |
| **Topics** | Artificial intelligence |
| **Products used in this lesson** | Red Hat OpenShift |
| **Lesson completion time** |  |

## Introduction

Now that the backend scripts have reported a success state, we need to verify that the operating system can see the newly created hardware layout.

To inspect the low-level hardware changes without leaving the cluster environment, run commands directly inside the device config manager (DCM) pod. In this lesson, you will use the built-in AMD System Management Interface (`amd-smi`) tool to confirm that the physical accelerator has successfully been partitioned according to the applied profile.

## Prerequisites

* Apply tolerations (lesson 1).    
* Configure and deploy the device config manager (lesson 2).   
* Taint and label GPU node (lesson 3). 

## In this lesson, you will:

* Use the user-space `amd-smi` tool inside the device config manager pod to verify that DCM has successfully partitioned the GPUs according to the profile.

## Verify GPU partitioning 

1. Get the DCM pod name:

```
DCM_POD=$(oc get pods -n openshift-amd-gpu \
  -l app.kubernetes.io/name=device-config-manager \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
```

2. With the container name saved, use `oc exec` to run a hardware inventory check and verify GPU partitioning with `amd-smi` . 

```
oc exec -n openshift-amd-gpu $DCM_POD -- amd-smi static list
```

   On a successfully partitioned AMD Instinct MI300X host configured for maximum density, you will see a text printout showing that your card has been divided. Instead of displaying just 8 physical cards, the driver list expands to show 64 devices (ranging from index 0 to 63). Example output in MI300X system:

   `GPU: 0`

       `BDF: 0000:1b:00.0`

       `UUID: 09ff74a1-0000-1000-802d-0540b39d66d6`

       `KFD_ID: 3771`

       `NODE_ID: 2`

       `PARTITION_ID: 0`

   

   `GPU: 1`

       `BDF: 0000:1b:00.1`

       `UUID: 04ff74a1-0000-1000-80b7-90c218050861`

       `KFD_ID: 62138`

       `NODE_ID: 3`

       `PARTITION_ID: 1`

   

   `... TRUNCATED ...`

   

   `GPU: 62`

       `BDF: 0000:dd:00.6`

       `UUID: 5cff74a1-0000-1000-80e7-da6c49d7b176`

       `KFD_ID: 32106`

       `NODE_ID: 64`

       `PARTITION_ID: 6`

   

   `GPU: 63`

       `BDF: 0000:dd:00.7`

       `UUID: 66ff74a1-0000-1000-809a-675c73e66337`

       `KFD_ID: 33131`

       `NODE_ID: 65`  
       `PARTITION_ID: 7`

3. Next, confirm the specific compute and memory partition modes reported by the hardware:

```
oc exec -n openshift-amd-gpu $DCM_POD -- amd-smi static --partition

```

   This diagnostic report should confirm that your physical hardware is running the proper Core Partition X (CPX) compute partition paired with the Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) Per Socket (NPS) 4 (NPS4) memory partition, giving you the highest possible workload density. Example output in MI300X system:

   `GPU: 0`

       `PARTITION:`

           `ACCELERATOR_PARTITION: CPX`

           `MEMORY_PARTITION: NPS4`

           `PARTITION_ID: 0`

   

   `GPU: 1`

       `PARTITION:`

           `ACCELERATOR_PARTITION: N/A`

           `MEMORY_PARTITION: N/A`

           `PARTITION_ID: 1`

   

   `... TRUNCATED ...`

   `GPU: 56`

       `PARTITION:`

           `ACCELERATOR_PARTITION: CPX`

           `MEMORY_PARTITION: NPS4`

           `PARTITION_ID: 0`

   

   `GPU: 57`

       `PARTITION:`

           `ACCELERATOR_PARTITION: N/A`

           `MEMORY_PARTITION: N/A`

           `PARTITION_ID: 1`

   

   `... TRUNCATED ...`

   

   `GPU: 63`

       `PARTITION:`

           `ACCELERATOR_PARTITION: N/A`

           `MEMORY_PARTITION: N/A`

           `PARTITION_ID: 7`

   

   **Note**: In a CPX \+ NPS4 configuration on an MI300X system, only `PARTITION_ID: 0` reports the active compute and memory mode; the remaining IDs show `N/A`.

Success\! You’ve verified that the single physical system is now operating as 64 devices. The hardware is partitioned and ready to schedule workloads.

In the next lesson, you will remove the node taint to open the host back up, allowing Red Hat OpenShift to start scheduling applications using your new hardware resources.

# Lesson 5: Untaint GPU node 

| Title *Describes job to be done* | Untaint GPU node |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Meta description** *160-character max summary of what they will learn, what will show in search engines* | Remove node taints and restore services.  |
| **Topics** | Artificial intelligence |
| **Products used in this lesson** | Red Hat OpenShift |
| **Lesson completion time** |  |

## Introduction

Now that you’ve successfully partitioned your hardware, you have to get your node added back to the cluster and accessible for scheduled workloads again. 

In this lesson, you will remove the node taint, adding the node back up to the cluster scheduler. You will also restore telemetry logging services with Prometheus exporter, giving us full visibility into your partitioned GPU resources.

## Prerequisites

* Verify GPU partitioning (lesson 4).

## In this lesson, you will:

* Remove taint from GPU node.  
* Restore telemetry logging services. 

## Untaint GPU node 

1. Run the following command to untaint the GPU node. Adding a minus sign (-) to the taint key tells Red Hat OpenShift to remove that taint from the node:

```
oc taint nodes $NODE_NAME amd-dcm=up:NoExecute-
```

2. Restore Prometheus exporter so it can resume scraping metrics from the newly partitioned devices:

```
oc patch prometheus amd-gpu-prometheus -n devmetrics --type='merge' -p '{"spec":{"replicas":1}}'
```

With the node untainted and the Prometheus exporter restored, the cluster is now fully operational under the new configuration. As seen in the updated dashboard (Figure 1), the MI300X system is successfully partitioned using the Core Partition X (CPX) compute profile paired with the Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) Per Socket (NPS) 4 (NPS4) memory profile, maximizing the available logical GPUs.

![][image2]  
Figure 1: MI300X System partitioned with CPX and NPS4 combination (maximum multi-tenancy partitioning).

Alt text: The same Grafana "AMD Instinct Single Node Dashboard" after CPX \+ NPS4 partitioning, now showing 64 logical GPUs (indices 0–63) instead of the original 8 physical devices, all healthy (green), at 0% utilization with \~20–83 MB memory each, confirming the partition profile was successfully applied.

Success\! You’ve removed the temporary scheduling blocks, restored telemetry logging, and verified that your Red Hat OpenShift cluster recognizes the maximum density configuration.

Now, let’s validate your workload using vLLM. 

# Lesson 6: Deploy a vLLM inference workload to validate GPU partitioning

## Introduction

Now that your AMD Instinct accelerators are successfully partitioned into 64 devices and ready for scheduling, you need to verify that applications can independently attach to these logical devices. 

To validate the newly partitioned setup, you will deploy a vLLM server to host a large language model. While the general process is similar to the official [vLLM documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/deployment/k8s/#deployment-with-cpushttps://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/deployment/k8s/#deployment-with-cpus), the following steps are specifically tailored for a Red Hat OpenShift environment using partitioned AMD Instinct GPUs.

## Prerequisites

* A successfully partitioned host (lesson 5).  
* Node restrictions removed and monitoring services restored (lesson 6).  
* Storage configured.  
* A [user access token](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/security-tokens) created in Hugging Face.

## In this lesson, you will:

* Provision Kubernetes storage and security manifests for an inference server.  
* Target a deployment to utilize a single partitioned amd.com/gpu resource.  
* Analyze memory and compute characteristics on a single partitioned slice.

## vLLM validation 

1. **Optional**: create a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) to store the model cache. In this learning path, we have used LVMS as the storage backend.

```
cat <<EOF | tee 01_pvc.yaml | oc apply -f -
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: vllm-models
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
  storageClassName: lvms-vg1
EOF
```

2. **Optional**: create a Kubernetes Secret (only required for accessing gated models in Hugging Face). 

```
cat <<EOF | tee 02_secret.yaml | oc apply -f -
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: hf-token
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: <hf_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx>
EOF
```

3. Create a deployment for vLLM. For this learning path, we use a small LLM model like meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for validation.

   **Note:** the `resources` section explicitly requests exactly one logical partition (`amd.com/gpu: "1"`):

```
cat <<EOF | tee 03_deployment.yaml | oc apply -f -
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: vllm
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: vllm-anyuid
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: system:openshift:scc:anyuid
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: vllm
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: vllm
  labels:
    app: vllm
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: vllm
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: vllm
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: vllm
      containers:
        - name: vllm
          image: docker.io/rocm/vllm:latest
          command:
            - python3
            - -m
            - vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server
            - --model
            - <model-name-goes-here>  # -> e.g. meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
            - --dtype
            - float16
            - --max-model-len
            - "4096"
            - --tensor-parallel-size
            - "1"
            - --host
            - "0.0.0.0"
            - --port
            - "8000"
          env:
            - name: HF_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: hf-token
                  key: token
            - name: HF_HOME
              value: /models
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
              name: http
          resources:
            requests:
              amd.com/gpu: "1"
              cpu: "4"
              memory: 16Gi
            limits:
              amd.com/gpu: "1"
              cpu: "8"
              memory: 32Gi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: models
              mountPath: /models
            - name: shm
              mountPath: /dev/shm
      volumes:
        - name: models
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: vllm-models
        - name: shm
          emptyDir:
            medium: Memory
            sizeLimit: 16Gi
      tolerations:
        - key: amd.com/gpu
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
EOF
```

4. **Optional**: create a service and route to expose the vLLM server to the outside world. Skip this step if you are not using a route to enable public access to the model. 

```
cat <<EOF | tee 04_service_route.yaml | oc apply -f -
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: vllm-server
  labels:
    app: vllm
spec:
  ports:
    - port: 8000
      targetPort: 8000
      name: http
  selector:
    app: vllm

---
apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: vllm-server
  labels:
    app: vllm
spec:
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: vllm-server
  port:
    targetPort: http
  tls:
    termination: edge
EOF
```

5. To test and validate the full deployment, use the exposed API and the deployed monitoring service:

```
VLLM_URL=$(oc get route vllm-server -o jsonpath='{.spec.host}')
```

7. Once the model is deployed and actively processing API requests, you can observe the immediate impact on your partitioned resources. The monitoring dashboard reveals that the memory allocated to this specific logical GPU is almost completely utilized by the model's weights and KV cache (Figure 1).

![][image3]

Figure 1: Dashboard view after deploying Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on a single CPX partition—GPU 0 consumes 2.2 GB for model weights and KV cache while all other partitions remain idle.

Alt text: Grafana dashboard showing a partitioned MI300X system serving a vLLM workload, where GPU 0 memory usage has jumped to 2.2 GB while the remaining 63 logical GPUs stay at \~20 MB, with a brief GPU utilization spike visible around 15:27 during inference.

8. Observe the GPU compute utilization behavior. Because this is an inference workload, the compute utilization does not sustain a constantly high load. Instead, it experiences a sharp, temporary bump during the short period of time it takes to process the prompt and generate the response (Figure 2).

![][image4]

Figure 2: Inference workload compute profile—GPU utilization spikes briefly to \~12% during prompt processing and token generation, then drops back to idle, while memory utilization remains constant at 3.43% holding the model weights.

Alt text: Grafana dashboard with three panels showing GPU utilization over time: average GPU utilization across all GPUs remains near 0% with a small blip around 15:27; average memory utilization holds steady at 3.43%; and the GPU utilization min/max/avg panel shows a brief bell-curve spike peaking at \~12% max around 15:27 before returning to 0%.

In this lesson, you deployed a single model occupying just one logical, partitioned GPU. However, this clearly demonstrates the massive scaling potential of this configuration. Because the Core Partition X (CPX) and NPS4 combination allows Kubernetes to recognize 64 GPUs as allocatable resources, this setup could (theoretically) scale to host 64 concurrent models on a single node.

# Learning path summary

The device config manager (DCM) on Red Hat OpenShift offers a robust way to make sure your high-end accelerators, like the AMD Instinct MI300X, aren’t being underutilized. By transitioning to advanced partitioning profiles, cluster administrators can drastically increase multi-tenant workload density.

When planning your deployments, remember that selecting optimal (and supported) GPU partitioning pairings—such as the Core Partition X (CPX) and Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) Per Socket (NPS) 4 (NPS4)  memory combination used in this learning path—is vital. 

By transforming a single physical GPU into up to 64 allocatable resources, you can achieve maximum concurrency, eliminate idle compute time, and scale your AI infrastructure.
